title: Chemistry 11 — Chapter 6: The Unknown Powder
description: An unlabeled white powder turned up in storage. Combustion analysis gave a percent composition — now it's up to you to work out what the compound actually is.

mika.name: Ms. Mika Tan
mika.description: Won't guess a compound's identity when the math can tell you for certain.

dev.name: Dev
dev.description: Wants to skip straight to the answer instead of working the ratios.

mole_notes.name: Mole Concept Notes
mole_notes.description: Avogadro's number, molar mass, and the n = m/M relationship.

composition_data.name: Combustion Analysis Data
composition_data.description: Percent composition by mass for the unknown powder.

elements.text: This jar has no label, just combustion analysis results — percent composition by mass. If we work the numbers correctly, we can identify exactly what's in it.
Can't we just smell it and guess?

elements.prompt: Mika hands you the mole concept notes.

options.text: "No — let's work through moles, percent composition, and the formula properly."
"Sure, let's just guess based on the smell."

elements.text: A mole is just a counting unit, like 'dozen,' but for atoms and molecules — specifically, 6.022 x 10^23 entities. That number is Avogadro's number.

config.question: Avogadro's number, 6.022 x 10^23, represents:

options.text: The number of entities (atoms, molecules, ions) in exactly one mole
The atomic mass of carbon-12
The molar volume of a gas at STP
The charge on a single electron

config.explanation: Avogadro's number defines the mole: exactly 6.022 x 10^23 entities per mole, regardless of what's being counted.

elements.text: Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol — you read it right off the periodic table. Moles, mass, and molar mass connect through n = m / M: moles equals mass divided by molar mass.

config.question: Which equation correctly relates moles (n), mass in grams (m), and molar mass (M)?

options.text: n = m / M
n = m x M
n = M / m
m = M / n

config.explanation: Moles = mass divided by molar mass. Rearranged, mass = moles x molar mass — not molar mass divided by moles.

config.prompt: Water's molar mass is 18.0 g/mol. How many moles are in 36.0 g of water?

elements.text: Percent composition tells you what fraction of a compound's mass comes from each element: (mass of that element / molar mass of the whole compound) times 100.

config.question: Percent composition tells you:

options.text: The mass fraction contributed by each element in a compound
The total number of moles in a sample
The molar volume of a gas at standard conditions
The empirical formula, without any further calculation

config.explanation: Percent composition is purely a mass-fraction breakdown — getting to a formula from it still takes another step.

config.prompt: Water, H2O, has a molar mass of 18.0 g/mol; the hydrogen in it contributes 2.0 g/mol. What percent of water's mass is hydrogen? (1 decimal place, no % sign)

elements.text: The jar's combustion analysis reads 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen, 53.3% oxygen. Assume a 100 g sample: that's 40.0 g C, 6.7 g H, 53.3 g O. Convert each to moles, then divide every value by the smallest one to get the simplest whole-number ratio.
C: 40.0 / 12.0 = 3.33 mol. H: 6.7 / 1.0 = 6.7 mol. O: 53.3 / 16.0 = 3.33 mol. Dividing all three by 3.33 gives a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio.

config.question: Why do you divide every element's mole count by the smallest one when finding an empirical formula?

options.text: To reduce the mole ratio down to the simplest whole numbers
To convert the moles back into grams
To calculate the molecular formula directly, skipping the empirical step
To find the compound's percent composition

config.explanation: Dividing by the smallest mole value normalizes the ratio so the smallest element becomes 1, giving the simplest whole-number ratio between all elements.

config.prompt: The mole ratio for C, H, and O works out to 1 : 2 : 1. What is the empirical formula? (e.g. CH2O style, no spaces)

elements.text: Not quite — that's the empirical formula, the simplest ratio. The actual molecule could be a whole-number multiple of it. We measured this powder's real molar mass separately: 180.0 g/mol. CH2O's own mass is 30.0 g/mol, so we divide 180.0 by 30.0 to find the multiplier.

config.prompt: Empirical formula mass = 30.0 g/mol; actual molar mass = 180.0 g/mol. What whole-number multiplier connects them?
Multiply every subscript in CH2O by 6. What is the molecular formula? (e.g. C6H12O6 style, no spaces)

elements.text: Glucose — C6H12O6. Every step checked out, from mole concept through to molecular formula. The jar gets a real label now.
We got there, but a few of those conversions were shaky. Let's tighten up the mole-to-formula chain before the next unknown.

elements.prompt: The jar is labeled. What now?

options.text: Walk Dev through the full chain — percent composition to empirical formula to molecular formula — one more time.
Label it and move on. Good enough for today.

elements.text: So percent composition gets you a ratio, the ratio gets you the empirical formula, and comparing molar masses tells you if the real molecule is bigger. Every unknown jar breaks down the same way.

ending.title: Formula Detective
ending.description: Identified the unknown powder as glucose from combustion data alone, and walked Dev through the full mole-to-formula chain.

ending.title: Jar Labeled
ending.description: The powder is identified and labeled. The deeper mole-to-formula chain can wait.
